facts.text: In spring 1845, the Stephens‑Townsend‑Murphy Party became the first wagon train to cross Emigrant Gap, guided by mountain man Caleb Greenwood.
Emigrant Gap earned California Historical Landmark No. 403 status in 1948, commemorating the pioneers who braved the Sierra Nevada.
At roughly 5,200 feet, Emigrant Gap serves as a low pass that separates the American River and Bear River drainages.
By the 1860s, a temporary stop at Emigrant Gap evolved into a permanent community thanks to railroad and stagecoach lines to California’s gold fields.
The first covered wagons to surmount the Sierra Nevada did so at Emigrant Gap in 1845, a milestone before the Gold Rush.
Gold mining began in the Emigrant Gap Mining District in the 1850s and continued intermittently into the 20th century.
